[[File:Sanjusangendo_Thousand-armed_Kannon.JPG|right|thumb|376x376px| Wooden seated Thousand-Armed Kannon statue owned by {{ill|Myōhō-in|ja|妙法院|de}} Temple (housed in Sanjusangendo Hall) {{ill|10=ja|11=国宝|A national treasure from|en|National Treasure (Japan)}} [[Kamakura period|the Kamakura period]] created by Tankei.]] [[File:Senju_Kannon.jpg|right|thumb|313x313px| A colored silk painting of the Thousand-Armed Kannon Statue, a national treasure from the late [[Heian period|Heian period,]] owned by [[Tokyo National Museum|the Tokyo National Museum]] .]]{{complex}} Thousand-Armed Avalokiteshvara (Senju Kannon, Sanskrit: सहस्रभुज, [{{Lang|sa|sahasrabhuja}}], Sahasrabhuja) is one of [[Bodhisattva|the bodhisattvas]] worshipped in [[Buddhism]] . [[en:draft:Sahasrabhuja]] "Sahasrabhuja" means "a thousand hands" or "one with a thousand hands". This name is also another name for [[Hinduism|Hindu]] gods such as [[Vishnu]], [[Shiva]], and the goddess [[Durga]], and is thought to be an incarnation of [[Guan Yin|the Bodhisattva Kannon]], who was established in [[India]] under the influence of Hinduism. It is also one of [[Guan Yin|the Six Kannon Bodhisattvas]] .
{{ill|10=ja|11=三昧耶形|The Sammaya form}} is an open lotus flower (a fully bloomed [[Nelumbo nucifera|lotus]] flower; it is paired with the first split lotus flower of {{ill|10=ja|11=聖観音|Āryāvalokiteśvara|en}} ) and a jewel on a lotus. The {{ill|10=ja|11=種子_(密教)|Bīja|lt=seed syllable|en|Bīja}} is Kirik (ह्रीः {{Lang|sa|hrīḥ}} ) <ref name="in">『印と真言の本』学研、2004th year 2月、p.99</ref> .
He has {{ill|5=vingt-huit légions|6=en:draft|8=zh|9=二十八部眾|10=ja|11=二十八部衆|28 legions|4=fr}} as his attendants.
She is part of {{Interlanguage link|12=draft|Kumano Gongen|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kumano Gongen|fr|6=en:draft}}. There is a 12 deity version, and a three deity version with {{ill|Amitabha|ja|阿弥陀如来|en}} {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|ja|薬師如来|en}} and {{ill|Sahasrabhuja|ja|千手観音|simple|User:Immanuelle/Sahasrabhuja|en|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Sahasrabhuja}}.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Gongen: Avatars of Japan's Mountain Sects, Shugendo, Shinto Traditions, & Syncretic Merging with Buddhist Deities|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/gongen-list-japan.html#KumanoSanshoGongen|access-date=2024-03-11|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref> [[fr:User:Immanuelle/Sahasrabhuja]] == The name and origin of "Senju" == As mentioned above, there are various names for the Thousand-Armed Kannon. Among the Thousand-Armed Kannon statues, there are some that have one or twenty-seven faces instead of eleven. Among these, the one-faced thousand-handed statue is considered to be an ancient form, and the one-faced thousand-handed statue in the 40th niche of Zhengshan, Danling, Sichuan Province, which is said to be the oldest surviving thousand-handed statue in China, is a one-faced thousand-handed statue. <ref>山岸公基「千手観音像に関する二、三の問題 経軌と８～９世紀の中国（四川省）・日本の作例をめぐって」『シルクロード学研究11 観音菩薩像の成立と展開 変化観音を中心にインドから日本まで』P129</ref> Under Japan's {{ill|5=Kulturgutschutzgesetz (Japan)|10=ja|11=文化財保護法|Cultural Properties Protection Law|4=de}}, the designated name for national treasures and [[Important Cultural Properties of Japan|important cultural properties]] is unified as "Thousand-Armed Kannon."
In the Garbha Mandala of [[Vajrayana|Esoteric Buddhism]], the place where Kannon are located is called the "Rengebu" <ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-09-26|title=大日如来の慈悲を表現した「胎蔵界」おさえておきたい曼荼羅の基本|url=https://discoverjapan-web.com/article/31151|access-date=2022-06-07|publisher=Discover Japan|和書}}</ref>, and among them, the Thousand-Armed Kannon is the highest-ranking being known as the "Renge-King Bodhisattva." This is the reason why Myoho-in {{ill|10=ja|11=三十三間堂|Sanjūsangen-dō|en|lt=Sanjūsangen-dō temple}} in Kyoto City is officially called Rengeo-in.
It is called by various names, such as 'Eleven-faced Thousand-armed Kannon,' 'Thousand-armed Thousand-eyed Kannon,' 'Eleven-faced Thousand-armed Thousand-eyed Kannon,' and 'Thousand-eyed Thousand-armed Kannon.' The name "Thousand Hands and a Thousand Eyes" comes from the fact that it is said to have one eye in each of its thousand hands. The thousand arms represent the immense mercy and power of Kannon, who seeks to save all living beings without exception. {{ill|10=ja|11=仏典|Buddhist texts|en}} that explains why Kannon Bodhisattva gained a thousand hands is the Thousand-Armed and Thousand-Eyed Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva's Vast, Perfect, Unhindered, and Great Compassionate Dharani Sutra, translated by Gabondharma. The {{ill|Great Compassion Mantra|en|Nīlakaṇṭha Dhāraṇī|fr|Nilakantha Dharani}} contained in this sutra is still recited today in {{ill|10=ja|11=天台宗|Tendai|en}} and [[Zen]] temples in China and Japan. As one of the six Kannon deities, it is said that he presides over {{ill|10=ja|11=餓鬼|lt=the realm of hungry ghosts|Hungry ghost|fr|Preta|en}} among the {{ill|Six_Paths|fr|Six destinées|lt=six realms of existence|en}} . It is also said that it saves people from the sufferings of [[hell]], represents the great utility of saving all living beings without obstacles, and is said to be in charge of the fulfillment of wishes and the birth of peaceful lives. [[ja:千手観音]] [[en:Sahasrabhuja]] [[fr:Sahasrabhuja]]
== Appearance == There are both seated and standing statues, and several surviving {{ill|10=ja|11=仏像|lt=Buddha statues|Buddha_in_art|en}} depicting around a thousand hands. Well-known examples include the statue (standing statue) in the Golden Hall of {{ill|10=ja|11=唐招提寺|Tōshōdai-ji|en}} in Nara City, the principal image (seated statue) of {{ill|10=ja|11=葛井寺|Fujii-dera|en|lt=Fujii-dera}} in Fujiidera City, Osaka Prefecture, and the principal image (standing statue) of Juho-ji Temple in Kyotanabe City, Kyoto Prefecture. The statues at Toshodaiji Temple, which are over 5 meters tall, have 42 main pillars and 911 small pillars between the gaps between the main pillars, making a total of 953 statues still extant. The statue at Katsurai-ji Temple has 40 large hands (without the bowl-shaped hands) and 1,001 small hands, for a total of 1,041 hands. <ref>[http://www.tnm.jp/modules/rblog/index.php/1/2018/02/14/%E5%8D%83%E6%89%8B%E8%A6%B3%E9%9F%B3%E8%8F%A9%E8%96%A9%E5%9D%90%E5%83%8F/ 天平の秘仏、葛井寺の国宝「千手観音菩薩坐像」がついに公開！]東京国立博物館（2018th year 2月14日）2018th year 3月18日閲覧。</ref> When viewed from the front, the gloves appear to grow directly from the statue itself, but in fact they are densely attached to two supports erected behind the statue. Faint traces reveal that eyes had been painted on the palms of the hands and knees of the Katsuraiji statue, literally representing "a thousand hands and a thousand eyes." [[ko:관세음보살]][[zh:千手千眼觀世音菩薩]] A typical Thousand-Armed Kannon statue has eleven faces and forty-two arms. The principal image of {{ill|10=ja|11=道成寺|Dōjō-ji|en|lt=Dojoji Temple}} (National Treasure) and the principal image of Fudarakusanji Temple (Important Cultural Property) in Wakayama Prefecture have 44 arms. The Thousand-Armed Kannon painting discovered in Dunhuang and kept at the British Museum and the Thousand-Armed Kannon standing statue kept at the Guimet Museum also have 44 arms. <ref>田中公明『千手観音と二十八部衆の謎』p87</ref> The meaning of the 42 arms is explained as follows: excluding the two hands clasped together in front of the chest, the 40 arms each represent saving 25 worlds, so "25 x 40 = 1,000." The "25 worlds" mentioned here refers to the " {{ill|10=ja|11=三界|Trailokya|en|lt=three realms}} {{ill|10=ja|11=二十五有|and twenty-five existences}} " in Buddhism, which is the idea that there are 25 worlds from heaven to hell (there are said to be 14 existences in the realm of desire, seven existences in the realm of form, and four existences in the realm of formlessness). The commonly used term " {{ill|10=ja|11=有頂天|Bhavāgra|en|lt=ecstatic}} " originally refers to the heavenly realm that is the pinnacle of the twenty-five levels of existence.
The principal image (seated statue) of Sanjusangendo Temple in Kyoto is a masterpiece by the Kamakura period Buddhist sculptor {{ill|10=ja|11=湛慶|Tankei|en}}, and is a typical example of an eleven-faced, forty-two-armed statue. Two of the forty-two hands are clasped together in front of the chest, and the other two are joined together in front of the stomach, holding [[宝鉢|a hohatsu]] (a sacred bowl) (called hohatsu-te). The other 38 arms each hold a different {{ill|10=ja|11=仏像|object}}, such as {{ill|10=ja|11=法輪|Dharmachakra|en|lt=a Dharma wheel}}, {{ill|10=ja|11=錫杖|Khakkhara|en|lt=a shakujo}} (a staff with a shaku), or {{ill|10=ja|11=水瓶|kuṇḍikā|lt=kuṇḍikā}} . What the 38 hands should hold is described in the sutras (see below), but in the case of statues, the objects have often been lost over the years or replaced with later additions.<gallery> File:La statue de Quan Am dans la pagode But Thap 2.jpg|link=File:La_statue_de_Quan_Am_dans_la_pagode_But_Thap_2.jpg|Vietnam, Butthap pagoda File:Buddha statue in Jade Buddha Temple 2.jpg|link=File:Buddha_statue_in_Jade_Buddha_Temple_2.jpg|Shanghai, Longhua Temple File:Thousand armed Kannon Hosshoji.JPG|link=File:Thousand_armed_Kannon_Hosshoji.JPG|Kyoto, Hoshoji Temple File:Senju Kannon Sanjusangendo.jpg|link=File:Senju_Kannon_Sanjusangendo.jpg|Kyoto, Sanjusangendo (out of 1,001 statues) File:Jiuhuashan bodhisattva image.jpg|link=File:Jiuhuashan_bodhisattva_image.jpg|Jiuhuashan, Anhui Province, China File:Статуя богини Гуаньинь в Чанше.jpg|link=File:Статуя_богини_Гуаньинь_в_Чанше.jpg|Huanshan, Hunan Province, China </gallery>
== Examples of beliefs and statues in Japan == There are few known examples of Thousand-Armed Kannon statues in India, but there are some in China, such as {{ill|10=ja|11=龍門石窟|Longmen_Grottoes|fr|Grottes_de_Longmen|en|lt=the Longmen Grottoes}} of the [[Tang dynasty|Tang Dynasty]] and {{ill|10=ja|11=大足石刻|Dazu_Rock_Carvings|fr|Sculptures_rupestres_de_Dazu|en|lt=the Dazu Rock Carvings}} of [[Song dynasty|the Song Dynasty]], both of which are [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Sites]] . Belief in the Thousand-Armed Kannon has a long history in Japan, with statues being made since the Nara period, before {{ill|10=ja|11=空海|Kūkai|en}} introduced the teachings of Esoteric Buddhism. It is known that [[千手堂|the Thousand-Armed Hall]] was built at [[Tōdai-ji|Todaiji Temple]] during the Tenpyo period, and a Thousand-Armed Kannon statue was also enshrined in the temple's lecture hall, which no longer exists. Of the surviving examples in Japan, the oldest is the Katsuo-ji Temple statue, which is thought to have been made in the mid-[[8th century]], and the Toshodaiji Temple statue was also made between the late 8th and early 9th centuries. A heavily damaged Thousand-Armed Kannon statue was discovered inside the inside of {{ill|10=ja|11=秘仏|Hibutsu|en|lt=the hidden}} Kitamuki Honzon statue at Dojoji Temple in Wakayama. This is thought to be the principal image of Dojoji Temple from its early days and dates back to the Nara period.
Other famous temples that enshrine the Thousand-Armed Kannon include [[Kiyomizu-dera|Kiyomizu-dera Temple]] and Sanjusangendo Temple in Kyoto City, and {{ill|10=ja|11=粉河寺|Kokawa-dera|en}} Temple (Kinokawa City, Wakayama Prefecture), one of the temples on the Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage. The principal image (standing statue) of Kiyomizu-dera Temple in Kyoto is a secret Buddha image that is only revealed to the public once every 33 years. It has a unique shape, with two of its 42 arms raised and clasped above its head, and is known as the "Kiyomizu-type" type. The secret Thousand-Armed Kannon statue, the principal image of Okunoin at the same Kiyomizu-dera temple, is a rare seated statue with 27 faces.
== The possession of the Thousand-Armed Kannon == The possessions of the Thousand-Armed Kannon are described in sutras such as the "Thousand-Armed Thousand-Eyed Dharani Sutra" (more specifically, the "Thousand-Armed Thousand-Eyed Kannon Bodhisattva's Vast, Perfect, Unobstructed, Great Compassionate Dharani Sutra"), and actual statues and images are generally designed according to these sutras.
For details on the following possessions, see Nishimura Kimitsune, "Buddha's World View" (Yoshikawa Kobunkan, 1980, [ page number required ] )by. Depending on the statue, the item described below as "held in the left hand" may be held in the right hand (or vice versa).
=== Left hand possession ===
* Hougeki: A staff-like object held in the left hand of the Thousand-Armed Kannon. A weapon with three prongs at its tip. * Kebutsu: A small Buddhist statue. * Houtaku: A small bell. * White lotus flower * Hossu: Originally a tool used to drive away flies and other insects. * A lasso. * The Sun Wheel (Nichirin) is referred to in the Sutra as "Nisshomani." * The Treasure Wheel Sutra states, "The Golden Wheel that Never Retreats." * A conch shell. * Gyokukan (jade ring) is also called "golden ring." Instead, they may carry a "treasure bracelet" (bracelet). * Skull staff * Gurenge * Bohai: A shield-like piece depicting the face of a dragon. * Palace (Kuuden) The scriptures refer to it as "Kuuden (Transformed Palace)." * It may also be held in the right hand. * The Hoko Sutra states that it is a "Kushi Iron Hook." A rod-shaped weapon with a bent tip at a right angle. * A sacred sword with a three-pronged handle. * The Hokyu (treasured bow) is paired with the arrow (Hoyan) held in the right hand. * Soubyou is also called "gunmochi." It means a pitcher of water.
=== Right hand possession ===
* The shakujo (seal staff) is paired with the "hogeki" (hogeki) held in the left hand. There are several rings attached to the top of the cane, and when you walk with it, the rings make a sound. It was originally used in India to ward off poisonous snakes when walking through the mountains and fields. * Kebutsu (transformed Buddha) * {{ill|10=ja|11=金剛杵|Vajra|en}}: A ritual implement with a handle in the center and three prongs on both ends. In the scriptures, the hand holding this is called 'basarashu'. * Blue lotus flower * Toothpick: A willow branch. Also known as willow. * Prayer {{ill|10=ja|11=数珠|Japamala|fr|Mâlâ|en|lt=beads}} * The Gachirin Sutra states that it is called "Gekseimani." * The Hoju (treasure jewel) is referred to in the Sutra as a "wish-granting jewel." * Also known as the Treasure Sutra (Hokyo) or the Sutra Box (Kyokyo). This refers to Buddhist scriptures. * Treasure seal * Budo refers to grapes. * Purple lotus * Semuishu: The hand that is not holding anything. * Treasured mirror * A small treasure chest. Also called 'Buddhist box'. * Vajra (kongosho) is also called 'tokkosho' (single-pronged vajra). A weapon with a central grip and sharp blades on both ends. * Axe (eppu) means "axe" or "axe". * This refers to a treasure arrow. * Kobyo: A Persian-style water pitcher. Also called "Treasure Aquarium."
In the Thousand-Armed Thousand-Eyed Dharani Sutra, in addition to the 38 hands holding objects mentioned above, 40 hands are mentioned, including the "prayer hands" and "treasure bowl hands." Looking at actual statues of the Thousand-Armed Kannon in Japan, many of them have their hands clasped in front of their stomachs (or on their knees in the case of seated statues), with a sacred bowl placed on top of them. The two hands holding the treasure bowls and the two hands clasped together in front of the chest total 42 arms.
== Mantra ==
* Ong Bazara Dalama (Dharma <ref name="in">『印と真言の本』学研、2004th year 2月、p.99</ref> ) and Kiriku <ref>市川智康 他『図解・仏像の見分け方』[[大法輪閣]]、1992nd year 、36頁。</ref>
== A representative Thousand-Armed Kannon statue in Japan == [[File:Senju_Kannon,_Toji_a085.jpg|thumb|225x225px| Toji Temple Old Dining Hall Statue]]

{{draft}} {{Promising draft|reason=the high amount of work put into it over a long time, see edit history}}
[[File:Sanjusangendo_Thousand-armed_Kannon.JPG|right|thumb|376x376px| Wooden seated Thousand-Armed Kannon statue owned by {{ill|Myōhō-in|ja|妙法院|de}} Temple (housed in Sanjusangendo Hall) {{ill|10=ja|11=国宝|A national treasure from|en|National Treasure (Japan)}} [[Kamakura period|the Kamakura period]] created by Tankei.]] [[File:Senju_Kannon.jpg|right|thumb|313x313px| A colored silk painting of the Thousand-Armed Kannon Statue, a national treasure from the late [[Heian period|Heian period,]] owned by [[Tokyo National Museum|the Tokyo National Museum]] .]]{{complex}} Thousand-Armed Avalokiteshvara (Senju Kannon, Sanskrit: सहस्रभुज, [{{Lang|sa|sahasrabhuja}}], Sahasrabhuja) is one of [[Bodhisattva|the bodhisattvas]] worshipped in [[Buddhism]] .
"Sahasrabhuja" means "a thousand hands" or "one with a thousand hands". This name is also another name for [[Hinduism|Hindu]] gods such as [[Vishnu]], [[Shiva]], and the goddess [[Durga]], and is thought to be an incarnation of [[Guan Yin|the Bodhisattva Kannon]], who was established in [[India]] under the influence of Hinduism. It is also one of [[Guan Yin|the Six Kannon Bodhisattvas]] .
{{ill|10=ja|11=三昧耶形|The Sammaya form}} is an open lotus flower (a fully bloomed [[Nelumbo nucifera|lotus]] flower; it is paired with the first split lotus flower of {{ill|10=ja|11=聖観音|Āryāvalokiteśvara|en}} ) and a jewel on a lotus. The {{ill|10=ja|11=種子_(密教)|Bīja|lt=seed syllable|en|Bīja}} is Kirik (ह्रीः {{Lang|sa|hrīḥ}} ) <ref name="in">『印と真言の本』学研、2004th year 2月、p.99</ref> .
He has {{ill|5=vingt-huit légions|6=en:draft|8=zh|9=二十八部眾|10=ja|11=二十八部衆|28 legions|4=fr}} as his attendants.
She is part of {{Interlanguage link|12=draft|Kumano Gongen|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kumano Gongen|fr|6=en:draft}}. There is a 12 deity version, and a three deity version with {{ill|Amitabha|ja|阿弥陀如来|en}} {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|ja|薬師如来|en}} and {{ill|Sahasrabhuja|ja|千手観音|simple|User:Immanuelle/Sahasrabhuja|en|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Sahasrabhuja}}.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Gongen: Avatars of Japan's Mountain Sects, Shugendo, Shinto Traditions, & Syncretic Merging with Buddhist Deities|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/gongen-list-japan.html#KumanoSanshoGongen|access-date=2024-03-11|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>
== The name and origin of "Senju" == As mentioned above, there are various names for the Thousand-Armed Kannon. Among the Thousand-Armed Kannon statues, there are some that have one or twenty-seven faces instead of eleven. Among these, the one-faced thousand-handed statue is considered to be an ancient form, and the one-faced thousand-handed statue in the 40th niche of Zhengshan, Danling, Sichuan Province, which is said to be the oldest surviving thousand-handed statue in China, is a one-faced thousand-handed statue. <ref>山岸公基「千手観音像に関する二、三の問題 経軌と８～９世紀の中国（四川省）・日本の作例をめぐって」『シルクロード学研究11 観音菩薩像の成立と展開 変化観音を中心にインドから日本まで』P129</ref> Under Japan's {{ill|5=Kulturgutschutzgesetz (Japan)|10=ja|11=文化財保護法|Cultural Properties Protection Law|4=de}}, the designated name for national treasures and [[Important Cultural Properties of Japan|important cultural properties]] is unified as "Thousand-Armed Kannon."
In the Garbha Mandala of [[Vajrayana|Esoteric Buddhism]], the place where Kannon are located is called the "Rengebu" <ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-09-26|title=大日如来の慈悲を表現した「胎蔵界」おさえておきたい曼荼羅の基本|url=https://discoverjapan-web.com/article/31151|access-date=2022-06-07|publisher=Discover Japan|和書}}</ref>, and among them, the Thousand-Armed Kannon is the highest-ranking being known as the "Renge-King Bodhisattva." This is the reason why Myoho-in {{ill|10=ja|11=三十三間堂|Sanjūsangen-dō|en|lt=Sanjūsangen-dō temple}} in Kyoto City is officially called Rengeo-in.
It is called by various names, such as 'Eleven-faced Thousand-armed Kannon,' 'Thousand-armed Thousand-eyed Kannon,' 'Eleven-faced Thousand-armed Thousand-eyed Kannon,' and 'Thousand-eyed Thousand-armed Kannon.' The name "Thousand Hands and a Thousand Eyes" comes from the fact that it is said to have one eye in each of its thousand hands. The thousand arms represent the immense mercy and power of Kannon, who seeks to save all living beings without exception. {{ill|10=ja|11=仏典|Buddhist texts|en}} that explains why Kannon Bodhisattva gained a thousand hands is the Thousand-Armed and Thousand-Eyed Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva's Vast, Perfect, Unhindered, and Great Compassionate Dharani Sutra, translated by Gabondharma. The {{ill|Great Compassion Mantra|en|Nīlakaṇṭha Dhāraṇī|fr|Nilakantha Dharani}} contained in this sutra is still recited today in {{ill|10=ja|11=天台宗|Tendai|en}} and [[Zen]] temples in China and Japan. As one of the six Kannon deities, it is said that he presides over {{ill|10=ja|11=餓鬼|lt=the realm of hungry ghosts|Hungry ghost|fr|Preta|en}} among the {{ill|Six_Paths|fr|Six destinées|lt=six realms of existence|en}} . It is also said that it saves people from the sufferings of [[hell]], represents the great utility of saving all living beings without obstacles, and is said to be in charge of the fulfillment of wishes and the birth of peaceful lives.
== Appearance == There are both seated and standing statues, and several surviving {{ill|10=ja|11=仏像|lt=Buddha statues|Buddha_in_art|en}} depicting around a thousand hands. Well-known examples include the statue (standing statue) in the Golden Hall of {{ill|10=ja|11=唐招提寺|Tōshōdai-ji|en}} in Nara City, the principal image (seated statue) of {{ill|10=ja|11=葛井寺|Fujii-dera|en|lt=Fujii-dera}} in Fujiidera City, Osaka Prefecture, and the principal image (standing statue) of Juho-ji Temple in Kyotanabe City, Kyoto Prefecture. The statues at Toshodaiji Temple, which are over 5 meters tall, have 42 main pillars and 911 small pillars between the gaps between the main pillars, making a total of 953 statues still extant. The statue at Katsurai-ji Temple has 40 large hands (without the bowl-shaped hands) and 1,001 small hands, for a total of 1,041 hands. <ref>[http://www.tnm.jp/modules/rblog/index.php/1/2018/02/14/%E5%8D%83%E6%89%8B%E8%A6%B3%E9%9F%B3%E8%8F%A9%E8%96%A9%E5%9D%90%E5%83%8F/ 天平の秘仏、葛井寺の国宝「千手観音菩薩坐像」がついに公開！]東京国立博物館（2018th year 2月14日）2018th year 3月18日閲覧。</ref> When viewed from the front, the gloves appear to grow directly from the statue itself, but in fact they are densely attached to two supports erected behind the statue. Faint traces reveal that eyes had been painted on the palms of the hands and knees of the Katsuraiji statue, literally representing "a thousand hands and a thousand eyes."
A typical Thousand-Armed Kannon statue has eleven faces and forty-two arms. The principal image of {{ill|10=ja|11=道成寺|Dōjō-ji|en|lt=Dojoji Temple}} (National Treasure) and the principal image of Fudarakusanji Temple (Important Cultural Property) in Wakayama Prefecture have 44 arms. The Thousand-Armed Kannon painting discovered in Dunhuang and kept at the British Museum and the Thousand-Armed Kannon standing statue kept at the Guimet Museum also have 44 arms. <ref>田中公明『千手観音と二十八部衆の謎』p87</ref> The meaning of the 42 arms is explained as follows: excluding the two hands clasped together in front of the chest, the 40 arms each represent saving 25 worlds, so "25 x 40 = 1,000." The "25 worlds" mentioned here refers to the " {{ill|10=ja|11=三界|Trailokya|en|lt=three realms}} {{ill|10=ja|11=二十五有|and twenty-five existences}} " in Buddhism, which is the idea that there are 25 worlds from heaven to hell (there are said to be 14 existences in the realm of desire, seven existences in the realm of form, and four existences in the realm of formlessness). The commonly used term " {{ill|10=ja|11=有頂天|Bhavāgra|en|lt=ecstatic}} " originally refers to the heavenly realm that is the pinnacle of the twenty-five levels of existence.
The principal image (seated statue) of Sanjusangendo Temple in Kyoto is a masterpiece by the Kamakura period Buddhist sculptor {{ill|10=ja|11=湛慶|Tankei|en}}, and is a typical example of an eleven-faced, forty-two-armed statue. Two of the forty-two hands are clasped together in front of the chest, and the other two are joined together in front of the stomach, holding [[宝鉢|a hohatsu]] (a sacred bowl) (called hohatsu-te). The other 38 arms each hold a different {{ill|10=ja|11=仏像|object}}, such as {{ill|10=ja|11=法輪|Dharmachakra|en|lt=a Dharma wheel}}, {{ill|10=ja|11=錫杖|Khakkhara|en|lt=a shakujo}} (a staff with a shaku), or {{ill|10=ja|11=水瓶|kuṇḍikā|lt=kuṇḍikā}} . What the 38 hands should hold is described in the sutras (see below), but in the case of statues, the objects have often been lost over the years or replaced with later additions.<gallery> File:La statue de Quan Am dans la pagode But Thap 2.jpg|link=File:La_statue_de_Quan_Am_dans_la_pagode_But_Thap_2.jpg|Vietnam, Butthap pagoda File:Buddha statue in Jade Buddha Temple 2.jpg|link=File:Buddha_statue_in_Jade_Buddha_Temple_2.jpg|Shanghai, Longhua Temple File:Thousand armed Kannon Hosshoji.JPG|link=File:Thousand_armed_Kannon_Hosshoji.JPG|Kyoto, Hoshoji Temple File:Senju Kannon Sanjusangendo.jpg|link=File:Senju_Kannon_Sanjusangendo.jpg|Kyoto, Sanjusangendo (out of 1,001 statues) File:Jiuhuashan bodhisattva image.jpg|link=File:Jiuhuashan_bodhisattva_image.jpg|Jiuhuashan, Anhui Province, China File:Статуя богини Гуаньинь в Чанше.jpg|link=File:Статуя_богини_Гуаньинь_в_Чанше.jpg|Huanshan, Hunan Province, China </gallery>
== Examples of beliefs and statues in Japan == There are few known examples of Thousand-Armed Kannon statues in India, but there are some in China, such as {{ill|10=ja|11=龍門石窟|Longmen_Grottoes|fr|Grottes_de_Longmen|en|lt=the Longmen Grottoes}} of the [[Tang dynasty|Tang Dynasty]] and {{ill|10=ja|11=大足石刻|Dazu_Rock_Carvings|fr|Sculptures_rupestres_de_Dazu|en|lt=the Dazu Rock Carvings}} of [[Song dynasty|the Song Dynasty]], both of which are [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Sites]] . Belief in the Thousand-Armed Kannon has a long history in Japan, with statues being made since the Nara period, before {{ill|10=ja|11=空海|Kūkai|en}} introduced the teachings of Esoteric Buddhism. It is known that [[千手堂|the Thousand-Armed Hall]] was built at [[Tōdai-ji|Todaiji Temple]] during the Tenpyo period, and a Thousand-Armed Kannon statue was also enshrined in the temple's lecture hall, which no longer exists. Of the surviving examples in Japan, the oldest is the Katsuo-ji Temple statue, which is thought to have been made in the mid-[[8th century]], and the Toshodaiji Temple statue was also made between the late 8th and early 9th centuries. A heavily damaged Thousand-Armed Kannon statue was discovered inside the inside of {{ill|10=ja|11=秘仏|Hibutsu|en|lt=the hidden}} Kitamuki Honzon statue at Dojoji Temple in Wakayama. This is thought to be the principal image of Dojoji Temple from its early days and dates back to the Nara period.
Other famous temples that enshrine the Thousand-Armed Kannon include [[Kiyomizu-dera|Kiyomizu-dera Temple]] and Sanjusangendo Temple in Kyoto City, and {{ill|10=ja|11=粉河寺|Kokawa-dera|en}} Temple (Kinokawa City, Wakayama Prefecture), one of the temples on the Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage. The principal image (standing statue) of Kiyomizu-dera Temple in Kyoto is a secret Buddha image that is only revealed to the public once every 33 years. It has a unique shape, with two of its 42 arms raised and clasped above its head, and is known as the "Kiyomizu-type" type. The secret Thousand-Armed Kannon statue, the principal image of Okunoin at the same Kiyomizu-dera temple, is a rare seated statue with 27 faces.
== The possession of the Thousand-Armed Kannon == The possessions of the Thousand-Armed Kannon are described in sutras such as the "Thousand-Armed Thousand-Eyed Dharani Sutra" (more specifically, the "Thousand-Armed Thousand-Eyed Kannon Bodhisattva's Vast, Perfect, Unobstructed, Great Compassionate Dharani Sutra"), and actual statues and images are generally designed according to these sutras.
For details on the following possessions, see Nishimura Kimitsune, "Buddha's World View" (Yoshikawa Kobunkan, 1980, [ page number required ] )by. Depending on the statue, the item described below as "held in the left hand" may be held in the right hand (or vice versa).
=== Left hand possession ===
* Hougeki: A staff-like object held in the left hand of the Thousand-Armed Kannon. A weapon with three prongs at its tip. * Kebutsu: A small Buddhist statue. * Houtaku: A small bell. * White lotus flower * Hossu: Originally a tool used to drive away flies and other insects. * A lasso. * The Sun Wheel (Nichirin) is referred to in the Sutra as "Nisshomani." * The Treasure Wheel Sutra states, "The Golden Wheel that Never Retreats." * A conch shell. * Gyokukan (jade ring) is also called "golden ring." Instead, they may carry a "treasure bracelet" (bracelet). * Skull staff * Gurenge * Bohai: A shield-like piece depicting the face of a dragon. * Palace (Kuuden) The scriptures refer to it as "Kuuden (Transformed Palace)." * It may also be held in the right hand. * The Hoko Sutra states that it is a "Kushi Iron Hook." A rod-shaped weapon with a bent tip at a right angle. * A sacred sword with a three-pronged handle. * The Hokyu (treasured bow) is paired with the arrow (Hoyan) held in the right hand. * Soubyou is also called "gunmochi." It means a pitcher of water.
=== Right hand possession ===
* The shakujo (seal staff) is paired with the "hogeki" (hogeki) held in the left hand. There are several rings attached to the top of the cane, and when you walk with it, the rings make a sound. It was originally used in India to ward off poisonous snakes when walking through the mountains and fields. * Kebutsu (transformed Buddha) * {{ill|10=ja|11=金剛杵|Vajra|en}}: A ritual implement with a handle in the center and three prongs on both ends. In the scriptures, the hand holding this is called 'basarashu'. * Blue lotus flower * Toothpick: A willow branch. Also known as willow. * Prayer {{ill|10=ja|11=数珠|Japamala|fr|Mâlâ|en|lt=beads}} * The Gachirin Sutra states that it is called "Gekseimani." * The Hoju (treasure jewel) is referred to in the Sutra as a "wish-granting jewel." * Also known as the Treasure Sutra (Hokyo) or the Sutra Box (Kyokyo). This refers to Buddhist scriptures. * Treasure seal * Budo refers to grapes. * Purple lotus * Semuishu: The hand that is not holding anything. * Treasured mirror * A small treasure chest. Also called 'Buddhist box'. * Vajra (kongosho) is also called 'tokkosho' (single-pronged vajra). A weapon with a central grip and sharp blades on both ends. * Axe (eppu) means "axe" or "axe". * This refers to a treasure arrow. * Kobyo: A Persian-style water pitcher. Also called "Treasure Aquarium."
In the Thousand-Armed Thousand-Eyed Dharani Sutra, in addition to the 38 hands holding objects mentioned above, 40 hands are mentioned, including the "prayer hands" and "treasure bowl hands." Looking at actual statues of the Thousand-Armed Kannon in Japan, many of them have their hands clasped in front of their stomachs (or on their knees in the case of seated statues), with a sacred bowl placed on top of them. The two hands holding the treasure bowls and the two hands clasped together in front of the chest total 42 arms.
== Mantra ==
* Ong Bazara Dalama (Dharma <ref name="in">『印と真言の本』学研、2004th year 2月、p.99</ref> ) and Kiriku <ref>市川智康 他『図解・仏像の見分け方』[[大法輪閣]]、1992nd year 、36頁。</ref>

{{draft}} {{Promising draft|reason=the high amount of work put into it over a long time, see edit history}}
[[File:Sanjusangendo_Thousand-armed_Kannon.JPG|right|thumb|376x376px| Wooden seated Thousand-Armed Kannon statue owned by {{ill|Myōhō-in|ja|妙法院|de|12=draft}} Temple (housed in Sanjusangendo Hall) {{ill|10=ja|11=国宝|A national treasure from|en|National Treasure (Japan)|12=draft}} [[Kamakura period|the Kamakura period]] created by Tankei.]] [[File:Senju_Kannon.jpg|right|thumb|313x313px| A colored silk painting of the Thousand-Armed Kannon Statue, a national treasure from the late [[Heian period|Heian period,]] owned by [[Tokyo National Museum|the Tokyo National Museum]] .]]{{complex}} Thousand-Armed Avalokiteshvara (Senju Kannon, Sanskrit: सहस्रभुज, [{{Lang|sa|sahasrabhuja}}], Sahasrabhuja) is one of [[Bodhisattva|the bodhisattvas]] worshipped in [[Buddhism]] .
"Sahasrabhuja" means "a thousand hands" or "one with a thousand hands". This name is also another name for [[Hinduism|Hindu]] gods such as [[Vishnu]], [[Shiva]], and the goddess [[Durga]], and is thought to be an incarnation of [[Guan Yin|the Bodhisattva Kannon]], who was established in [[India]] under the influence of Hinduism. It is also one of [[Guan Yin|the Six Kannon Bodhisattvas]] .
{{ill|10=ja|11=三昧耶形|The Sammaya form|12=draft}} is an open lotus flower (a fully bloomed [[Nelumbo nucifera|lotus]] flower; it is paired with the first split lotus flower of {{ill|10=ja|11=聖観音|Āryāvalokiteśvara|en|12=draft}} ) and a jewel on a lotus. The {{ill|10=ja|11=種子_(密教)|Bīja|lt=seed syllable|en|Bīja|12=draft}} is Kirik (ह्रीः {{Lang|sa|hrīḥ}} ) <ref name="in">『印と真言の本』学研、2004th year 2月、p.99</ref> .
He has {{ill|5=vingt-huit légions|6=en:draft|8=zh|9=二十八部眾|10=ja|11=二十八部衆|28 legions|4=fr|12=draft}} as his attendants.
She is part of {{Interlanguage link|12=draft|Kumano Gongen|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kumano Gongen|fr|6=en:draft}}. There is a 12 deity version, and a three deity version with {{ill|Amitabha|ja|阿弥陀如来|en|12=draft}} {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|ja|薬師如来|en|12=draft}} and {{ill|Sahasrabhuja|ja|千手観音|simple|User:Immanuelle/Sahasrabhuja|en|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Sahasrabhuja|12=draft}}.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Gongen: Avatars of Japan's Mountain Sects, Shugendo, Shinto Traditions, & Syncretic Merging with Buddhist Deities|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/gongen-list-japan.html#KumanoSanshoGongen|access-date=2024-03-11|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>
== The name and origin of "Senju" == As mentioned above, there are various names for the Thousand-Armed Kannon. Among the Thousand-Armed Kannon statues, there are some that have one or twenty-seven faces instead of eleven. Among these, the one-faced thousand-handed statue is considered to be an ancient form, and the one-faced thousand-handed statue in the 40th niche of Zhengshan, Danling, Sichuan Province, which is said to be the oldest surviving thousand-handed statue in China, is a one-faced thousand-handed statue. <ref>山岸公基「千手観音像に関する二、三の問題 経軌と８～９世紀の中国（四川省）・日本の作例をめぐって」『シルクロード学研究11 観音菩薩像の成立と展開 変化観音を中心にインドから日本まで』P129</ref> Under Japan's {{ill|5=Kulturgutschutzgesetz (Japan)|10=ja|11=文化財保護法|Cultural Properties Protection Law|4=de|12=draft}}, the designated name for national treasures and [[Important Cultural Properties of Japan|important cultural properties]] is unified as "Thousand-Armed Kannon."
In the Garbha Mandala of [[Vajrayana|Esoteric Buddhism]], the place where Kannon are located is called the "Rengebu" <ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-09-26|title=大日如来の慈悲を表現した「胎蔵界」おさえておきたい曼荼羅の基本|url=https://discoverjapan-web.com/article/31151|access-date=2022-06-07|publisher=Discover Japan|和書}}</ref>, and among them, the Thousand-Armed Kannon is the highest-ranking being known as the "Renge-King Bodhisattva." This is the reason why Myoho-in {{ill|10=ja|11=三十三間堂|Sanjūsangen-dō|en|lt=Sanjūsangen-dō temple|12=draft}} in Kyoto City is officially called Rengeo-in.
It is called by various names, such as 'Eleven-faced Thousand-armed Kannon,' 'Thousand-armed Thousand-eyed Kannon,' 'Eleven-faced Thousand-armed Thousand-eyed Kannon,' and 'Thousand-eyed Thousand-armed Kannon.' The name "Thousand Hands and a Thousand Eyes" comes from the fact that it is said to have one eye in each of its thousand hands. The thousand arms represent the immense mercy and power of Kannon, who seeks to save all living beings without exception. {{ill|10=ja|11=仏典|Buddhist texts|en|12=draft}} that explains why Kannon Bodhisattva gained a thousand hands is the Thousand-Armed and Thousand-Eyed Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva's Vast, Perfect, Unhindered, and Great Compassionate Dharani Sutra, translated by Gabondharma. The {{ill|Great Compassion Mantra|en|Nīlakaṇṭha Dhāraṇī|fr|Nilakantha Dharani|12=draft}} contained in this sutra is still recited today in {{ill|10=ja|11=天台宗|Tendai|en|12=draft}} and [[Zen]] temples in China and Japan. As one of the six Kannon deities, it is said that he presides over {{ill|10=ja|11=餓鬼|lt=the realm of hungry ghosts|Hungry ghost|fr|Preta|en|12=draft}} among the {{ill|Six_Paths|fr|Six destinées|lt=six realms of existence|en|12=draft}} . It is also said that it saves people from the sufferings of [[hell]], represents the great utility of saving all living beings without obstacles, and is said to be in charge of the fulfillment of wishes and the birth of peaceful lives.
== Appearance == There are both seated and standing statues, and several surviving {{ill|10=ja|11=仏像|lt=Buddha statues|Buddha_in_art|en|12=draft}} depicting around a thousand hands. Well-known examples include the statue (standing statue) in the Golden Hall of {{ill|10=ja|11=唐招提寺|Tōshōdai-ji|en|12=draft}} in Nara City, the principal image (seated statue) of {{ill|10=ja|11=葛井寺|Fujii-dera|en|lt=Fujii-dera|12=draft}} in Fujiidera City, Osaka Prefecture, and the principal image (standing statue) of Juho-ji Temple in Kyotanabe City, Kyoto Prefecture. The statues at Toshodaiji Temple, which are over 5 meters tall, have 42 main pillars and 911 small pillars between the gaps between the main pillars, making a total of 953 statues still extant. The statue at Katsurai-ji Temple has 40 large hands (without the bowl-shaped hands) and 1,001 small hands, for a total of 1,041 hands. <ref>[http://www.tnm.jp/modules/rblog/index.php/1/2018/02/14/%E5%8D%83%E6%89%8B%E8%A6%B3%E9%9F%B3%E8%8F%A9%E8%96%A9%E5%9D%90%E5%83%8F/ 天平の秘仏、葛井寺の国宝「千手観音菩薩坐像」がついに公開！]東京国立博物館（2018th year 2月14日）2018th year 3月18日閲覧。</ref> When viewed from the front, the gloves appear to grow directly from the statue itself, but in fact they are densely attached to two supports erected behind the statue. Faint traces reveal that eyes had been painted on the palms of the hands and knees of the Katsuraiji statue, literally representing "a thousand hands and a thousand eyes."
A typical Thousand-Armed Kannon statue has eleven faces and forty-two arms. The principal image of {{ill|10=ja|11=道成寺|Dōjō-ji|en|lt=Dojoji Temple|12=draft}} (National Treasure) and the principal image of Fudarakusanji Temple (Important Cultural Property) in Wakayama Prefecture have 44 arms. The Thousand-Armed Kannon painting discovered in Dunhuang and kept at the British Museum and the Thousand-Armed Kannon standing statue kept at the Guimet Museum also have 44 arms. <ref>田中公明『千手観音と二十八部衆の謎』p87</ref> The meaning of the 42 arms is explained as follows: excluding the two hands clasped together in front of the chest, the 40 arms each represent saving 25 worlds, so "25 x 40 = 1,000." The "25 worlds" mentioned here refers to the " {{ill|10=ja|11=三界|Trailokya|en|lt=three realms|12=draft}} {{ill|10=ja|11=二十五有|and twenty-five existences|12=draft}} " in Buddhism, which is the idea that there are 25 worlds from heaven to hell (there are said to be 14 existences in the realm of desire, seven existences in the realm of form, and four existences in the realm of formlessness). The commonly used term " {{ill|10=ja|11=有頂天|Bhavāgra|en|lt=ecstatic|12=draft}} " originally refers to the heavenly realm that is the pinnacle of the twenty-five levels of existence.
The principal image (seated statue) of Sanjusangendo Temple in Kyoto is a masterpiece by the Kamakura period Buddhist sculptor {{ill|10=ja|11=湛慶|Tankei|en|12=draft}}, and is a typical example of an eleven-faced, forty-two-armed statue. Two of the forty-two hands are clasped together in front of the chest, and the other two are joined together in front of the stomach, holding [[宝鉢|a hohatsu]] (a sacred bowl) (called hohatsu-te). The other 38 arms each hold a different {{ill|10=ja|11=仏像|object|12=draft}}, such as {{ill|10=ja|11=法輪|Dharmachakra|en|lt=a Dharma wheel|12=draft}}, {{ill|10=ja|11=錫杖|Khakkhara|en|lt=a shakujo|12=draft}} (a staff with a shaku), or {{ill|10=ja|11=水瓶|kuṇḍikā|lt=kuṇḍikā|12=draft}} . What the 38 hands should hold is described in the sutras (see below), but in the case of statues, the objects have often been lost over the years or replaced with later additions.<gallery> File:La statue de Quan Am dans la pagode But Thap 2.jpg|link=File:La_statue_de_Quan_Am_dans_la_pagode_But_Thap_2.jpg|Vietnam, Butthap pagoda File:Buddha statue in Jade Buddha Temple 2.jpg|link=File:Buddha_statue_in_Jade_Buddha_Temple_2.jpg|Shanghai, Longhua Temple File:Thousand armed Kannon Hosshoji.JPG|link=File:Thousand_armed_Kannon_Hosshoji.JPG|Kyoto, Hoshoji Temple File:Senju Kannon Sanjusangendo.jpg|link=File:Senju_Kannon_Sanjusangendo.jpg|Kyoto, Sanjusangendo (out of 1,001 statues) File:Jiuhuashan bodhisattva image.jpg|link=File:Jiuhuashan_bodhisattva_image.jpg|Jiuhuashan, Anhui Province, China File:Статуя богини Гуаньинь в Чанше.jpg|link=File:Статуя_богини_Гуаньинь_в_Чанше.jpg|Huanshan, Hunan Province, China </gallery>
== Examples of beliefs and statues in Japan == There are few known examples of Thousand-Armed Kannon statues in India, but there are some in China, such as {{ill|10=ja|11=龍門石窟|Longmen_Grottoes|fr|Grottes_de_Longmen|en|lt=the Longmen Grottoes|12=draft}} of the [[Tang dynasty|Tang Dynasty]] and {{ill|10=ja|11=大足石刻|Dazu_Rock_Carvings|fr|Sculptures_rupestres_de_Dazu|en|lt=the Dazu Rock Carvings|12=draft}} of [[Song dynasty|the Song Dynasty]], both of which are [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Sites]] . Belief in the Thousand-Armed Kannon has a long history in Japan, with statues being made since the Nara period, before {{ill|10=ja|11=空海|Kūkai|en|12=draft}} introduced the teachings of Esoteric Buddhism. It is known that [[千手堂|the Thousand-Armed Hall]] was built at [[Tōdai-ji|Todaiji Temple]] during the Tenpyo period, and a Thousand-Armed Kannon statue was also enshrined in the temple's lecture hall, which no longer exists. Of the surviving examples in Japan, the oldest is the Katsuo-ji Temple statue, which is thought to have been made in the mid-[[8th century]], and the Toshodaiji Temple statue was also made between the late 8th and early 9th centuries. A heavily damaged Thousand-Armed Kannon statue was discovered inside the inside of {{ill|10=ja|11=秘仏|Hibutsu|en|lt=the hidden|12=draft}} Kitamuki Honzon statue at Dojoji Temple in Wakayama. This is thought to be the principal image of Dojoji Temple from its early days and dates back to the Nara period.
Other famous temples that enshrine the Thousand-Armed Kannon include [[Kiyomizu-dera|Kiyomizu-dera Temple]] and Sanjusangendo Temple in Kyoto City, and {{ill|10=ja|11=粉河寺|Kokawa-dera|en|12=draft}} Temple (Kinokawa City, Wakayama Prefecture), one of the temples on the Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage. The principal image (standing statue) of Kiyomizu-dera Temple in Kyoto is a secret Buddha image that is only revealed to the public once every 33 years. It has a unique shape, with two of its 42 arms raised and clasped above its head, and is known as the "Kiyomizu-type" type. The secret Thousand-Armed Kannon statue, the principal image of Okunoin at the same Kiyomizu-dera temple, is a rare seated statue with 27 faces.
== The possession of the Thousand-Armed Kannon == The possessions of the Thousand-Armed Kannon are described in sutras such as the "Thousand-Armed Thousand-Eyed Dharani Sutra" (more specifically, the "Thousand-Armed Thousand-Eyed Kannon Bodhisattva's Vast, Perfect, Unobstructed, Great Compassionate Dharani Sutra"), and actual statues and images are generally designed according to these sutras.
For details on the following possessions, see Nishimura Kimitsune, "Buddha's World View" (Yoshikawa Kobunkan, 1980, [ page number required ] )by. Depending on the statue, the item described below as "held in the left hand" may be held in the right hand (or vice versa).
=== Left hand possession ===
* Hougeki: A staff-like object held in the left hand of the Thousand-Armed Kannon. A weapon with three prongs at its tip. * Kebutsu: A small Buddhist statue. * Houtaku: A small bell. * White lotus flower * Hossu: Originally a tool used to drive away flies and other insects. * A lasso. * The Sun Wheel (Nichirin) is referred to in the Sutra as "Nisshomani." * The Treasure Wheel Sutra states, "The Golden Wheel that Never Retreats." * A conch shell. * Gyokukan (jade ring) is also called "golden ring." Instead, they may carry a "treasure bracelet" (bracelet). * Skull staff * Gurenge * Bohai: A shield-like piece depicting the face of a dragon. * Palace (Kuuden) The scriptures refer to it as "Kuuden (Transformed Palace)." * It may also be held in the right hand. * The Hoko Sutra states that it is a "Kushi Iron Hook." A rod-shaped weapon with a bent tip at a right angle. * A sacred sword with a three-pronged handle. * The Hokyu (treasured bow) is paired with the arrow (Hoyan) held in the right hand. * Soubyou is also called "gunmochi." It means a pitcher of water.
=== Right hand possession ===
* The shakujo (seal staff) is paired with the "hogeki" (hogeki) held in the left hand. There are several rings attached to the top of the cane, and when you walk with it, the rings make a sound. It was originally used in India to ward off poisonous snakes when walking through the mountains and fields. * Kebutsu (transformed Buddha) * {{ill|10=ja|11=金剛杵|Vajra|en|12=draft}}: A ritual implement with a handle in the center and three prongs on both ends. In the scriptures, the hand holding this is called 'basarashu'. * Blue lotus flower * Toothpick: A willow branch. Also known as willow. * Prayer {{ill|10=ja|11=数珠|Japamala|fr|Mâlâ|en|lt=beads|12=draft}} * The Gachirin Sutra states that it is called "Gekseimani." * The Hoju (treasure jewel) is referred to in the Sutra as a "wish-granting jewel." * Also known as the Treasure Sutra (Hokyo) or the Sutra Box (Kyokyo). This refers to Buddhist scriptures. * Treasure seal * Budo refers to grapes. * Purple lotus * Semuishu: The hand that is not holding anything. * Treasured mirror * A small treasure chest. Also called 'Buddhist box'. * Vajra (kongosho) is also called 'tokkosho' (single-pronged vajra). A weapon with a central grip and sharp blades on both ends. * Axe (eppu) means "axe" or "axe". * This refers to a treasure arrow. * Kobyo: A Persian-style water pitcher. Also called "Treasure Aquarium."
In the Thousand-Armed Thousand-Eyed Dharani Sutra, in addition to the 38 hands holding objects mentioned above, 40 hands are mentioned, including the "prayer hands" and "treasure bowl hands." Looking at actual statues of the Thousand-Armed Kannon in Japan, many of them have their hands clasped in front of their stomachs (or on their knees in the case of seated statues), with a sacred bowl placed on top of them. The two hands holding the treasure bowls and the two hands clasped together in front of the chest total 42 arms.

[[File:Sanjusangendo_Thousand-armed_Kannon.JPG|right|thumb|376x376px| Wooden seated Thousand-Armed Kannon statue owned by {{ill|Myōhō-in|ja|妙法院|de|12=draft}} Temple (housed in Sanjusangendo Hall) {{ill|10=ja|11=国宝|A national treasure from|en|National Treasure (Japan)|12=draft}} [[Kamakura period|the Kamakura period]] created by Tankei.]] [[File:Senju_Kannon.jpg|right|thumb|313x313px| A colored silk painting of the Thousand-Armed Kannon Statue, a national treasure from the late [[Heian period|Heian period,]] owned by [[Tokyo National Museum|the Tokyo National Museum]] .]]{{complex}} Thousand-Armed Avalokiteshvara (Senju Kannon, Sanskrit: सहस्रभुज, [{{Lang|sa|sahasrabhuja}}], Sahasrabhuja) is one of [[Bodhisattva|the bodhisattvas]] worshipped in [[Buddhism]] .
"Sahasrabhuja" means "a thousand hands" or "one with a thousand hands". This name is also another name for [[Hinduism|Hindu]] gods such as [[Vishnu]], [[Shiva]], and the goddess [[Durga]], and is thought to be an incarnation of [[Guan Yin|the Bodhisattva Kannon]], who was established in [[India]] under the influence of Hinduism. It is also one of [[Guan Yin|the Six Kannon Bodhisattvas]] .
{{ill|10=ja|11=三昧耶形|The Sammaya form|12=draft}} is an open lotus flower (a fully bloomed [[Nelumbo nucifera|lotus]] flower; it is paired with the first split lotus flower of {{ill|10=ja|11=聖観音|Āryāvalokiteśvara|en|12=draft}} ) and a jewel on a lotus. The {{ill|10=ja|11=種子_(密教)|Bīja|lt=seed syllable|en|Bīja|12=draft}} is Kirik (ह्रीः {{Lang|sa|hrīḥ}} ) <ref name="in">『印と真言の本』学研、2004th year 2月、p.99</ref> .
He has {{ill|5=vingt-huit légions|6=en:draft|8=zh|9=二十八部眾|10=ja|11=二十八部衆|28 legions|4=fr|12=draft}} as his attendants.
She is part of {{Interlanguage link|12=draft|Kumano Gongen|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kumano Gongen|fr|6=en:draft}}. There is a 12 deity version, and a three deity version with {{ill|Amitabha|ja|阿弥陀如来|en|12=draft}} {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|ja|薬師如来|en|12=draft}} and {{ill|Sahasrabhuja|ja|千手観音|simple|User:Immanuelle/Sahasrabhuja|en|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Sahasrabhuja|12=draft}}.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Gongen: Avatars of Japan's Mountain Sects, Shugendo, Shinto Traditions, & Syncretic Merging with Buddhist Deities|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/gongen-list-japan.html#KumanoSanshoGongen|access-date=2024-03-11|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>
== The name and origin of "Senju" == As mentioned above, there are various names for the Thousand-Armed Kannon. Among the Thousand-Armed Kannon statues, there are some that have one or twenty-seven faces instead of eleven. Among these, the one-faced thousand-handed statue is considered to be an ancient form, and the one-faced thousand-handed statue in the 40th niche of Zhengshan, Danling, Sichuan Province, which is said to be the oldest surviving thousand-handed statue in China, is a one-faced thousand-handed statue. <ref>山岸公基「千手観音像に関する二、三の問題 経軌と８～９世紀の中国（四川省）・日本の作例をめぐって」『シルクロード学研究11 観音菩薩像の成立と展開 変化観音を中心にインドから日本まで』P129</ref> Under Japan's {{ill|5=Kulturgutschutzgesetz (Japan)|10=ja|11=文化財保護法|Cultural Properties Protection Law|4=de|12=draft}}, the designated name for national treasures and [[Important Cultural Properties of Japan|important cultural properties]] is unified as "Thousand-Armed Kannon."
In the Garbha Mandala of [[Vajrayana|Esoteric Buddhism]], the place where Kannon are located is called the "Rengebu" <ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-09-26|title=大日如来の慈悲を表現した「胎蔵界」おさえておきたい曼荼羅の基本|url=https://discoverjapan-web.com/article/31151|access-date=2022-06-07|publisher=Discover Japan|和書}}</ref>, and among them, the Thousand-Armed Kannon is the highest-ranking being known as the "Renge-King Bodhisattva." This is the reason why Myoho-in {{ill|10=ja|11=三十三間堂|Sanjūsangen-dō|en|lt=Sanjūsangen-dō temple|12=draft}} in Kyoto City is officially called Rengeo-in.
It is called by various names, such as 'Eleven-faced Thousand-armed Kannon,' 'Thousand-armed Thousand-eyed Kannon,' 'Eleven-faced Thousand-armed Thousand-eyed Kannon,' and 'Thousand-eyed Thousand-armed Kannon.' The name "Thousand Hands and a Thousand Eyes" comes from the fact that it is said to have one eye in each of its thousand hands. The thousand arms represent the immense mercy and power of Kannon, who seeks to save all living beings without exception. {{ill|10=ja|11=仏典|Buddhist texts|en|12=draft}} that explains why Kannon Bodhisattva gained a thousand hands is the Thousand-Armed and Thousand-Eyed Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva's Vast, Perfect, Unhindered, and Great Compassionate Dharani Sutra, translated by Gabondharma. The {{ill|Great Compassion Mantra|en|Nīlakaṇṭha Dhāraṇī|fr|Nilakantha Dharani|12=draft}} contained in this sutra is still recited today in {{ill|10=ja|11=天台宗|Tendai|en|12=draft}} and [[Zen]] temples in China and Japan. As one of the six Kannon deities, it is said that he presides over {{ill|10=ja|11=餓鬼|lt=the realm of hungry ghosts|Hungry ghost|fr|Preta|en|12=draft}} among the {{ill|Six_Paths|fr|Six destinées|lt=six realms of existence|en|12=draft}} . It is also said that it saves people from the sufferings of [[hell]], represents the great utility of saving all living beings without obstacles, and is said to be in charge of the fulfillment of wishes and the birth of peaceful lives.
== Appearance == There are both seated and standing statues, and several surviving {{ill|10=ja|11=仏像|lt=Buddha statues|Buddha_in_art|en|12=draft}} depicting around a thousand hands. Well-known examples include the statue (standing statue) in the Golden Hall of {{ill|10=ja|11=唐招提寺|Tōshōdai-ji|en|12=draft}} in Nara City, the principal image (seated statue) of {{ill|10=ja|11=葛井寺|Fujii-dera|en|lt=Fujii-dera|12=draft}} in Fujiidera City, Osaka Prefecture, and the principal image (standing statue) of Juho-ji Temple in Kyotanabe City, Kyoto Prefecture. The statues at Toshodaiji Temple, which are over 5 meters tall, have 42 main pillars and 911 small pillars between the gaps between the main pillars, making a total of 953 statues still extant. The statue at Katsurai-ji Temple has 40 large hands (without the bowl-shaped hands) and 1,001 small hands, for a total of 1,041 hands. <ref>[http://www.tnm.jp/modules/rblog/index.php/1/2018/02/14/%E5%8D%83%E6%89%8B%E8%A6%B3%E9%9F%B3%E8%8F%A9%E8%96%A9%E5%9D%90%E5%83%8F/ 天平の秘仏、葛井寺の国宝「千手観音菩薩坐像」がついに公開！]東京国立博物館（2018th year 2月14日）2018th year 3月18日閲覧。</ref> When viewed from the front, the gloves appear to grow directly from the statue itself, but in fact they are densely attached to two supports erected behind the statue. Faint traces reveal that eyes had been painted on the palms of the hands and knees of the Katsuraiji statue, literally representing "a thousand hands and a thousand eyes."
A typical Thousand-Armed Kannon statue has eleven faces and forty-two arms. The principal image of {{ill|10=ja|11=道成寺|Dōjō-ji|en|lt=Dojoji Temple|12=draft}} (National Treasure) and the principal image of Fudarakusanji Temple (Important Cultural Property) in Wakayama Prefecture have 44 arms. The Thousand-Armed Kannon painting discovered in Dunhuang and kept at the British Museum and the Thousand-Armed Kannon standing statue kept at the Guimet Museum also have 44 arms. <ref>田中公明『千手観音と二十八部衆の謎』p87</ref> The meaning of the 42 arms is explained as follows: excluding the two hands clasped together in front of the chest, the 40 arms each represent saving 25 worlds, so "25 x 40 = 1,000." The "25 worlds" mentioned here refers to the " {{ill|10=ja|11=三界|Trailokya|en|lt=three realms|12=draft}} {{ill|10=ja|11=二十五有|and twenty-five existences|12=draft}} " in Buddhism, which is the idea that there are 25 worlds from heaven to hell (there are said to be 14 existences in the realm of desire, seven existences in the realm of form, and four existences in the realm of formlessness). The commonly used term " {{ill|10=ja|11=有頂天|Bhavāgra|en|lt=ecstatic|12=draft}} " originally refers to the heavenly realm that is the pinnacle of the twenty-five levels of existence.
The principal image (seated statue) of Sanjusangendo Temple in Kyoto is a masterpiece by the Kamakura period Buddhist sculptor {{ill|10=ja|11=湛慶|Tankei|en|12=draft}}, and is a typical example of an eleven-faced, forty-two-armed statue. Two of the forty-two hands are clasped together in front of the chest, and the other two are joined together in front of the stomach, holding [[宝鉢|a hohatsu]] (a sacred bowl) (called hohatsu-te). The other 38 arms each hold a different {{ill|10=ja|11=仏像|object|12=draft}}, such as {{ill|10=ja|11=法輪|Dharmachakra|en|lt=a Dharma wheel|12=draft}}, {{ill|10=ja|11=錫杖|Khakkhara|en|lt=a shakujo|12=draft}} (a staff with a shaku), or {{ill|10=ja|11=水瓶|kuṇḍikā|lt=kuṇḍikā|12=draft}} . What the 38 hands should hold is described in the sutras (see below), but in the case of statues, the objects have often been lost over the years or replaced with later additions.<gallery> File:La statue de Quan Am dans la pagode But Thap 2.jpg|link=File:La_statue_de_Quan_Am_dans_la_pagode_But_Thap_2.jpg|Vietnam, Butthap pagoda File:Buddha statue in Jade Buddha Temple 2.jpg|link=File:Buddha_statue_in_Jade_Buddha_Temple_2.jpg|Shanghai, Longhua Temple File:Thousand armed Kannon Hosshoji.JPG|link=File:Thousand_armed_Kannon_Hosshoji.JPG|Kyoto, Hoshoji Temple File:Senju Kannon Sanjusangendo.jpg|link=File:Senju_Kannon_Sanjusangendo.jpg|Kyoto, Sanjusangendo (out of 1,001 statues) File:Jiuhuashan bodhisattva image.jpg|link=File:Jiuhuashan_bodhisattva_image.jpg|Jiuhuashan, Anhui Province, China File:Статуя богини Гуаньинь в Чанше.jpg|link=File:Статуя_богини_Гуаньинь_в_Чанше.jpg|Huanshan, Hunan Province, China </gallery>
== Examples of beliefs and statues in Japan == There are few known examples of Thousand-Armed Kannon statues in India, but there are some in China, such as {{ill|10=ja|11=龍門石窟|Longmen_Grottoes|fr|Grottes_de_Longmen|en|lt=the Longmen Grottoes|12=draft}} of the [[Tang dynasty|Tang Dynasty]] and {{ill|10=ja|11=大足石刻|Dazu_Rock_Carvings|fr|Sculptures_rupestres_de_Dazu|en|lt=the Dazu Rock Carvings|12=draft}} of [[Song dynasty|the Song Dynasty]], both of which are [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Sites]] . Belief in the Thousand-Armed Kannon has a long history in Japan, with statues being made since the Nara period, before {{ill|10=ja|11=空海|Kūkai|en|12=draft}} introduced the teachings of Esoteric Buddhism. It is known that [[千手堂|the Thousand-Armed Hall]] was built at [[Tōdai-ji|Todaiji Temple]] during the Tenpyo period, and a Thousand-Armed Kannon statue was also enshrined in the temple's lecture hall, which no longer exists. Of the surviving examples in Japan, the oldest is the Katsuo-ji Temple statue, which is thought to have been made in the mid-[[8th century]], and the Toshodaiji Temple statue was also made between the late 8th and early 9th centuries. A heavily damaged Thousand-Armed Kannon statue was discovered inside the inside of {{ill|10=ja|11=秘仏|Hibutsu|en|lt=the hidden|12=draft}} Kitamuki Honzon statue at Dojoji Temple in Wakayama. This is thought to be the principal image of Dojoji Temple from its early days and dates back to the Nara period.
Other famous temples that enshrine the Thousand-Armed Kannon include [[Kiyomizu-dera|Kiyomizu-dera Temple]] and Sanjusangendo Temple in Kyoto City, and {{ill|10=ja|11=粉河寺|Kokawa-dera|en|12=draft}} Temple (Kinokawa City, Wakayama Prefecture), one of the temples on the Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage. The principal image (standing statue) of Kiyomizu-dera Temple in Kyoto is a secret Buddha image that is only revealed to the public once every 33 years. It has a unique shape, with two of its 42 arms raised and clasped above its head, and is known as the "Kiyomizu-type" type. The secret Thousand-Armed Kannon statue, the principal image of Okunoin at the same Kiyomizu-dera temple, is a rare seated statue with 27 faces.
== The possession of the Thousand-Armed Kannon == The possessions of the Thousand-Armed Kannon are described in sutras such as the "Thousand-Armed Thousand-Eyed Dharani Sutra" (more specifically, the "Thousand-Armed Thousand-Eyed Kannon Bodhisattva's Vast, Perfect, Unobstructed, Great Compassionate Dharani Sutra"), and actual statues and images are generally designed according to these sutras.
For details on the following possessions, see Nishimura Kimitsune, "Buddha's World View" (Yoshikawa Kobunkan, 1980, [ page number required ] )by. Depending on the statue, the item described below as "held in the left hand" may be held in the right hand (or vice versa).
=== Left hand possession ===
* Hougeki: A staff-like object held in the left hand of the Thousand-Armed Kannon. A weapon with three prongs at its tip. * Kebutsu: A small Buddhist statue. * Houtaku: A small bell. * White lotus flower * Hossu: Originally a tool used to drive away flies and other insects. * A lasso. * The Sun Wheel (Nichirin) is referred to in the Sutra as "Nisshomani." * The Treasure Wheel Sutra states, "The Golden Wheel that Never Retreats." * A conch shell. * Gyokukan (jade ring) is also called "golden ring." Instead, they may carry a "treasure bracelet" (bracelet). * Skull staff * Gurenge * Bohai: A shield-like piece depicting the face of a dragon. * Palace (Kuuden) The scriptures refer to it as "Kuuden (Transformed Palace)." * It may also be held in the right hand. * The Hoko Sutra states that it is a "Kushi Iron Hook." A rod-shaped weapon with a bent tip at a right angle. * A sacred sword with a three-pronged handle. * The Hokyu (treasured bow) is paired with the arrow (Hoyan) held in the right hand. * Soubyou is also called "gunmochi." It means a pitcher of water.
=== Right hand possession ===
* The shakujo (seal staff) is paired with the "hogeki" (hogeki) held in the left hand. There are several rings attached to the top of the cane, and when you walk with it, the rings make a sound. It was originally used in India to ward off poisonous snakes when walking through the mountains and fields. * Kebutsu (transformed Buddha) * {{ill|10=ja|11=金剛杵|Vajra|en|12=draft}}: A ritual implement with a handle in the center and three prongs on both ends. In the scriptures, the hand holding this is called 'basarashu'. * Blue lotus flower * Toothpick: A willow branch. Also known as willow. * Prayer {{ill|10=ja|11=数珠|Japamala|fr|Mâlâ|en|lt=beads|12=draft}} * The Gachirin Sutra states that it is called "Gekseimani." * The Hoju (treasure jewel) is referred to in the Sutra as a "wish-granting jewel." * Also known as the Treasure Sutra (Hokyo) or the Sutra Box (Kyokyo). This refers to Buddhist scriptures. * Treasure seal * Budo refers to grapes. * Purple lotus * Semuishu: The hand that is not holding anything. * Treasured mirror * A small treasure chest. Also called 'Buddhist box'. * Vajra (kongosho) is also called 'tokkosho' (single-pronged vajra). A weapon with a central grip and sharp blades on both ends. * Axe (eppu) means "axe" or "axe". * This refers to a treasure arrow. * Kobyo: A Persian-style water pitcher. Also called "Treasure Aquarium."
In the Thousand-Armed Thousand-Eyed Dharani Sutra, in addition to the 38 hands holding objects mentioned above, 40 hands are mentioned, including the "prayer hands" and "treasure bowl hands." Looking at actual statues of the Thousand-Armed Kannon in Japan, many of them have their hands clasped in front of their stomachs (or on their knees in the case of seated statues), with a sacred bowl placed on top of them. The two hands holding the treasure bowls and the two hands clasped together in front of the chest total 42 arms.

[[File:Sanjusangendo_Thousand-armed_Kannon.JPG|right|thumb|376x376px| Wooden seated Thousand-Armed Kannon statue owned by {{ill|Myōhō-in|ja|妙法院|de|12=draft}} Temple (housed in Sanjusangendo Hall) {{ill|10=ja|11=国宝|A national treasure from|en|National Treasure (Japan)|12=draft}} [[Kamakura period|the Kamakura period]] created by Tankei.]] [[File:Senju_Kannon.jpg|right|thumb|313x313px| A colored silk painting of the Thousand-Armed Kannon Statue, a national treasure from the late [[Heian period|Heian period,]] owned by [[Tokyo National Museum|the Tokyo National Museum]] .]]{{complex}} Thousand-Armed Avalokiteshvara (Senju Kannon, Sanskrit: सहस्रभुज, [{{Lang|sa|sahasrabhuja}}], Sahasrabhuja) is one of [[Bodhisattva|the bodhisattvas]] worshipped in [[Buddhism]] .
"Sahasrabhuja" means "a thousand hands" or "one with a thousand hands". This name is also another name for [[Hinduism|Hindu]] gods such as [[Vishnu]], [[Shiva]], and the goddess [[Durga]], and is thought to be an incarnation of [[Guan Yin|the Bodhisattva Kannon]], who was established in [[India]] under the influence of Hinduism. It is also one of [[Guan Yin|the Six Kannon Bodhisattvas]] .
{{ill|10=ja|11=三昧耶形|The Sammaya form|12=draft}} is an open lotus flower (a fully bloomed [[Nelumbo nucifera|lotus]] flower; it is paired with the first split lotus flower of {{ill|10=ja|11=聖観音|Āryāvalokiteśvara|en|12=draft}} ) and a jewel on a lotus. The {{ill|10=ja|11=種子_(密教)|Bīja|lt=seed syllable|en|Bīja|12=draft}} is Kirik (ह्रीः {{Lang|sa|hrīḥ}} ) <ref name="in">『印と真言の本』学研、2004th year 2月、p.99</ref> .
He has {{ill|5=vingt-huit légions|6=en:draft|8=zh|9=二十八部眾|10=ja|11=二十八部衆|28 legions|4=fr|12=draft}} as his attendants.
She is part of {{Interlanguage link|12=draft|Kumano Gongen|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kumano Gongen|fr|6=en:draft}}. There is a 12 deity version, and a three deity version with {{ill|Amitabha|ja|阿弥陀如来|en|12=draft}} {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|ja|薬師如来|en|12=draft}} and {{ill|Sahasrabhuja|ja|千手観音|simple|User:Immanuelle/Sahasrabhuja|en|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Sahasrabhuja|12=draft}}.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Gongen: Avatars of Japan's Mountain Sects, Shugendo, Shinto Traditions, & Syncretic Merging with Buddhist Deities|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/gongen-list-japan.html#KumanoSanshoGongen|access-date=2024-03-11|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>
== The name and origin of "Senju" == As mentioned above, there are various names for the Thousand-Armed Kannon. Among the Thousand-Armed Kannon statues, there are some that have one or twenty-seven faces instead of eleven. Among these, the one-faced thousand-handed statue is considered to be an ancient form, and the one-faced thousand-handed statue in the 40th niche of Zhengshan, Danling, Sichuan Province, which is said to be the oldest surviving thousand-handed statue in China, is a one-faced thousand-handed statue. <ref>山岸公基「千手観音像に関する二、三の問題 経軌と８～９世紀の中国（四川省）・日本の作例をめぐって」『シルクロード学研究11 観音菩薩像の成立と展開 変化観音を中心にインドから日本まで』P129</ref> Under Japan's {{ill|5=Kulturgutschutzgesetz (Japan)|10=ja|11=文化財保護法|Cultural Properties Protection Law|4=de|12=draft}}, the designated name for national treasures and [[Important Cultural Properties of Japan|important cultural properties]] is unified as "Thousand-Armed Kannon."
In the Garbha Mandala of [[Vajrayana|Esoteric Buddhism]], the place where Kannon are located is called the "Rengebu" <ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-09-26|title=大日如来の慈悲を表現した「胎蔵界」おさえておきたい曼荼羅の基本|url=https://discoverjapan-web.com/article/31151|access-date=2022-06-07|publisher=Discover Japan|和書}}</ref>, and among them, the Thousand-Armed Kannon is the highest-ranking being known as the "Renge-King Bodhisattva." This is the reason why Myoho-in {{ill|10=ja|11=三十三間堂|Sanjūsangen-dō|en|lt=Sanjūsangen-dō temple|12=draft}} in Kyoto City is officially called Rengeo-in.
It is called by various names, such as 'Eleven-faced Thousand-armed Kannon,' 'Thousand-armed Thousand-eyed Kannon,' 'Eleven-faced Thousand-armed Thousand-eyed Kannon,' and 'Thousand-eyed Thousand-armed Kannon.' The name "Thousand Hands and a Thousand Eyes" comes from the fact that it is said to have one eye in each of its thousand hands. The thousand arms represent the immense mercy and power of Kannon, who seeks to save all living beings without exception. {{ill|10=ja|11=仏典|Buddhist texts|en|12=draft}} that explains why Kannon Bodhisattva gained a thousand hands is the Thousand-Armed and Thousand-Eyed Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva's Vast, Perfect, Unhindered, and Great Compassionate Dharani Sutra, translated by Gabondharma. The {{ill|Great Compassion Mantra|en|Nīlakaṇṭha Dhāraṇī|fr|Nilakantha Dharani|12=draft}} contained in this sutra is still recited today in {{ill|10=ja|11=天台宗|Tendai|en|12=draft}} and [[Zen]] temples in China and Japan. As one of the six Kannon deities, it is said that he presides over {{ill|10=ja|11=餓鬼|lt=the realm of hungry ghosts|Hungry ghost|fr|Preta|en|12=draft}} among the {{ill|Six_Paths|fr|Six destinées|lt=six realms of existence|en|12=draft}} . It is also said that it saves people from the sufferings of [[hell]], represents the great utility of saving all living beings without obstacles, and is said to be in charge of the fulfillment of wishes and the birth of peaceful lives.
== Appearance == There are both seated and standing statues, and several surviving {{ill|10=ja|11=仏像|lt=Buddha statues|Buddha_in_art|en|12=draft}} depicting around a thousand hands. Well-known examples include the statue (standing statue) in the Golden Hall of {{ill|10=ja|11=唐招提寺|Tōshōdai-ji|en|12=draft}} in Nara City, the principal image (seated statue) of {{ill|10=ja|11=葛井寺|Fujii-dera|en|lt=Fujii-dera|12=draft}} in Fujiidera City, Osaka Prefecture, and the principal image (standing statue) of Juho-ji Temple in Kyotanabe City, Kyoto Prefecture. The statues at Toshodaiji Temple, which are over 5 meters tall, have 42 main pillars and 911 small pillars between the gaps between the main pillars, making a total of 953 statues still extant. The statue at Katsurai-ji Temple has 40 large hands (without the bowl-shaped hands) and 1,001 small hands, for a total of 1,041 hands. <ref>[http://www.tnm.jp/modules/rblog/index.php/1/2018/02/14/%E5%8D%83%E6%89%8B%E8%A6%B3%E9%9F%B3%E8%8F%A9%E8%96%A9%E5%9D%90%E5%83%8F/ 天平の秘仏、葛井寺の国宝「千手観音菩薩坐像」がついに公開！]東京国立博物館（2018th year 2月14日）2018th year 3月18日閲覧。</ref> When viewed from the front, the gloves appear to grow directly from the statue itself, but in fact they are densely attached to two supports erected behind the statue. Faint traces reveal that eyes had been painted on the palms of the hands and knees of the Katsuraiji statue, literally representing "a thousand hands and a thousand eyes."
A typical Thousand-Armed Kannon statue has eleven faces and forty-two arms. The principal image of {{ill|10=ja|11=道成寺|Dōjō-ji|en|lt=Dojoji Temple|12=draft}} (National Treasure) and the principal image of Fudarakusanji Temple (Important Cultural Property) in Wakayama Prefecture have 44 arms. The Thousand-Armed Kannon painting discovered in Dunhuang and kept at the British Museum and the Thousand-Armed Kannon standing statue kept at the Guimet Museum also have 44 arms. <ref>田中公明『千手観音と二十八部衆の謎』p87</ref> The meaning of the 42 arms is explained as follows: excluding the two hands clasped together in front of the chest, the 40 arms each represent saving 25 worlds, so "25 x 40 = 1,000." The "25 worlds" mentioned here refers to the " {{ill|10=ja|11=三界|Trailokya|en|lt=three realms|12=draft}} {{ill|10=ja|11=二十五有|and twenty-five existences|12=draft}} " in Buddhism, which is the idea that there are 25 worlds from heaven to hell (there are said to be 14 existences in the realm of desire, seven existences in the realm of form, and four existences in the realm of formlessness). The commonly used term " {{ill|10=ja|11=有頂天|Bhavāgra|en|lt=ecstatic|12=draft}} " originally refers to the heavenly realm that is the pinnacle of the twenty-five levels of existence.
The principal image (seated statue) of Sanjusangendo Temple in Kyoto is a masterpiece by the Kamakura period Buddhist sculptor {{ill|10=ja|11=湛慶|Tankei|en|12=draft}}, and is a typical example of an eleven-faced, forty-two-armed statue. Two of the forty-two hands are clasped together in front of the chest, and the other two are joined together in front of the stomach, holding [[宝鉢|a hohatsu]] (a sacred bowl) (called hohatsu-te). The other 38 arms each hold a different {{ill|10=ja|11=仏像|object|12=draft}}, such as {{ill|10=ja|11=法輪|Dharmachakra|en|lt=a Dharma wheel|12=draft}}, {{ill|10=ja|11=錫杖|Khakkhara|en|lt=a shakujo|12=draft}} (a staff with a shaku), or {{ill|10=ja|11=水瓶|kuṇḍikā|lt=kuṇḍikā|12=draft}} . What the 38 hands should hold is described in the sutras (see below), but in the case of statues, the objects have often been lost over the years or replaced with later additions.<gallery> File:La statue de Quan Am dans la pagode But Thap 2.jpg|link=File:La_statue_de_Quan_Am_dans_la_pagode_But_Thap_2.jpg|Vietnam, Butthap pagoda File:Buddha statue in Jade Buddha Temple 2.jpg|link=File:Buddha_statue_in_Jade_Buddha_Temple_2.jpg|Shanghai, Longhua Temple File:Thousand armed Kannon Hosshoji.JPG|link=File:Thousand_armed_Kannon_Hosshoji.JPG|Kyoto, Hoshoji Temple File:Senju Kannon Sanjusangendo.jpg|link=File:Senju_Kannon_Sanjusangendo.jpg|Kyoto, Sanjusangendo (out of 1,001 statues) File:Jiuhuashan bodhisattva image.jpg|link=File:Jiuhuashan_bodhisattva_image.jpg|Jiuhuashan, Anhui Province, China File:Статуя богини Гуаньинь в Чанше.jpg|link=File:Статуя_богини_Гуаньинь_в_Чанше.jpg|Huanshan, Hunan Province, China </gallery>
== Examples of beliefs and statues in Japan == There are few known examples of Thousand-Armed Kannon statues in India, but there are some in China, such as {{ill|10=ja|11=龍門石窟|Longmen_Grottoes|fr|Grottes_de_Longmen|en|lt=the Longmen Grottoes|12=draft}} of the [[Tang dynasty|Tang Dynasty]] and {{ill|10=ja|11=大足石刻|Dazu_Rock_Carvings|fr|Sculptures_rupestres_de_Dazu|en|lt=the Dazu Rock Carvings|12=draft}} of [[Song dynasty|the Song Dynasty]], both of which are [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Sites]] . Belief in the Thousand-Armed Kannon has a long history in Japan, with statues being made since the Nara period, before {{ill|10=ja|11=空海|Kūkai|en|12=draft}} introduced the teachings of Esoteric Buddhism. It is known that [[千手堂|the Thousand-Armed Hall]] was built at [[Tōdai-ji|Todaiji Temple]] during the Tenpyo period, and a Thousand-Armed Kannon statue was also enshrined in the temple's lecture hall, which no longer exists. Of the surviving examples in Japan, the oldest is the Katsuo-ji Temple statue, which is thought to have been made in the mid-[[8th century]], and the Toshodaiji Temple statue was also made between the late 8th and early 9th centuries. A heavily damaged Thousand-Armed Kannon statue was discovered inside the inside of {{ill|10=ja|11=秘仏|Hibutsu|en|lt=the hidden|12=draft}} Kitamuki Honzon statue at Dojoji Temple in Wakayama. This is thought to be the principal image of Dojoji Temple from its early days and dates back to the Nara period.
Other famous temples that enshrine the Thousand-Armed Kannon include [[Kiyomizu-dera|Kiyomizu-dera Temple]] and Sanjusangendo Temple in Kyoto City, and {{ill|10=ja|11=粉河寺|Kokawa-dera|en|12=draft}} Temple (Kinokawa City, Wakayama Prefecture), one of the temples on the Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage. The principal image (standing statue) of Kiyomizu-dera Temple in Kyoto is a secret Buddha image that is only revealed to the public once every 33 years. It has a unique shape, with two of its 42 arms raised and clasped above its head, and is known as the "Kiyomizu-type" type. The secret Thousand-Armed Kannon statue, the principal image of Okunoin at the same Kiyomizu-dera temple, is a rare seated statue with 27 faces.
== The possession of the Thousand-Armed Kannon == The possessions of the Thousand-Armed Kannon are described in sutras such as the "Thousand-Armed Thousand-Eyed Dharani Sutra" (more specifically, the "Thousand-Armed Thousand-Eyed Kannon Bodhisattva's Vast, Perfect, Unobstructed, Great Compassionate Dharani Sutra"), and actual statues and images are generally designed according to these sutras.
For details on the following possessions, see Nishimura Kimitsune, "Buddha's World View" (Yoshikawa Kobunkan, 1980, [ page number required ] )by. Depending on the statue, the item described below as "held in the left hand" may be held in the right hand (or vice versa).
=== Left hand possession ===
* Hougeki: A staff-like object held in the left hand of the Thousand-Armed Kannon. A weapon with three prongs at its tip. * Kebutsu: A small Buddhist statue. * Houtaku: A small bell. * White lotus flower * Hossu: Originally a tool used to drive away flies and other insects. * A lasso. * The Sun Wheel (Nichirin) is referred to in the Sutra as "Nisshomani." * The Treasure Wheel Sutra states, "The Golden Wheel that Never Retreats." * A conch shell. * Gyokukan (jade ring) is also called "golden ring." Instead, they may carry a "treasure bracelet" (bracelet). * Skull staff * Gurenge * Bohai: A shield-like piece depicting the face of a dragon. * Palace (Kuuden) The scriptures refer to it as "Kuuden (Transformed Palace)." * It may also be held in the right hand. * The Hoko Sutra states that it is a "Kushi Iron Hook." A rod-shaped weapon with a bent tip at a right angle. * A sacred sword with a three-pronged handle. * The Hokyu (treasured bow) is paired with the arrow (Hoyan) held in the right hand. * Soubyou is also called "gunmochi." It means a pitcher of water.
=== Right hand possession ===
* The shakujo (seal staff) is paired with the "hogeki" (hogeki) held in the left hand. There are several rings attached to the top of the cane, and when you walk with it, the rings make a sound. It was originally used in India to ward off poisonous snakes when walking through the mountains and fields. * Kebutsu (transformed Buddha) * {{ill|10=ja|11=金剛杵|Vajra|en|12=draft}}: A ritual implement with a handle in the center and three prongs on both ends. In the scriptures, the hand holding this is called 'basarashu'. * Blue lotus flower * Toothpick: A willow branch. Also known as willow. * Prayer {{ill|10=ja|11=数珠|Japamala|fr|Mâlâ|en|lt=beads|12=draft}} * The Gachirin Sutra states that it is called "Gekseimani." * The Hoju (treasure jewel) is referred to in the Sutra as a "wish-granting jewel." * Also known as the Treasure Sutra (Hokyo) or the Sutra Box (Kyokyo). This refers to Buddhist scriptures. * Treasure seal * Budo refers to grapes. * Purple lotus * Semuishu: The hand that is not holding anything. * Treasured mirror * A small treasure chest. Also called 'Buddhist box'. * Vajra (kongosho) is also called 'tokkosho' (single-pronged vajra). A weapon with a central grip and sharp blades on both ends. * Axe (eppu) means "axe" or "axe". * This refers to a treasure arrow. * Kobyo: A Persian-style water pitcher. Also called "Treasure Aquarium."
In the Thousand-Armed Thousand-Eyed Dharani Sutra, in addition to the 38 hands holding objects mentioned above, 40 hands are mentioned, including the "prayer hands" and "treasure bowl hands." Looking at actual statues of the Thousand-Armed Kannon in Japan, many of them have their hands clasped in front of their stomachs (or on their knees in the case of seated statues), with a sacred bowl placed on top of them. The two hands holding the treasure bowls and the two hands clasped together in front of the chest total 42 arms.
